# On Onuris: a letter to a colleague

*A letter to a colleague, 31 July 2026 — on the name Onuris, and on the forms that keep failing it.*

Your note said, roughly: surely the marks are a nicety. Permit me to use Onuris to show they are not.

First, the attestation. The attested form is **𓏎𓈖𓁷𓂋𓏏𓈐𓅆**, from the tradition's own record. The canonical transliteration is **Onuris**.

Say it aloud as the sources heard it: “ON-yoor-iss” The marks are what carry that sound to a reader who has never heard it spoken.

On the plain form — and I want to be precise, because you pushed on this. The plain form *onuris* differs from the canonical *Onuris* only by convention of display — case, not content. It is *acceptable everywhere*: in legacy systems, in plain-text citation, in the DNS itself. What is not acceptable is what follows in the register: respellings that change the letters, not just their case.

One more thing, because it always surprises: the name did not stay home. Onuris is the Thinite doublet of Shu: same retrieval-myth, same air-theology, localised and armed.  The Greeks knew him as Anuris and left him largely unmapped — no Olympian quite covered ‘the husband who fetches’ — while Egyptian theology folded him contentedly into the greater Shu.

And it never stopped working. His myth survives as one of the most charming of the Eye-cycle variants — the only one where the divine embassy ends in marriage.  The Thinite nome’s devotion to him outlasted its political weight by millennia; and his name, in the Greek form Anuris, wandered into the magical papyri as a word of power for recovering what is lost.

## The Convention's Own History

Egyptological transliteration exists because hieroglyphs write consonants, not vowels. The characters ꜣ (aleph) and ꜥ (ayin) are consonants — a glottal reed and a pharyngeal grip — and rendering them as vowels does not "simplify" the name, it deletes consonants from it. The conventions in use descend from nineteenth-century decipherment and the standardized Manuel de Codage: ḥ, ḫ, ḏ, ṯ each mark a distinct consonant the Egyptian wrote and a modern reader must not merge. When this register defends them, it defends the principle that a writing system older than the alphabet gets to keep its consonants.

## The Address, Without an Encoding Detour

The canonical form **Onuris** already uses ordinary Latin letters, so the address bar needs no special encoding narrative. The digital temple can preserve the spelling exactly as the scholarly record presents it. That is the practical point here: consistency between the source, the citation, and the public address.

This does not make every romanization equally valid. A wrong letter remains wrong even when it is easy to type. Canonical status still depends on the attested convention, never on convenience or registrar inventory.

Write back when you have checked the sources; they are better company than I am.

*— The Register*

## The Verdict

**Onuris** is the canonical form: attested, checkable, and enforced across the temple, the lexicon, the cards, the APIs, and this register. The plain form *onuris* shares that standing — the two are the same name in every system. The false forms above are documented so that no reader has to take the temple's word on faith — the violations are stated, the sources are named, and the register stands open to challenge on every line.

The temple of **Onuris** stands at [/onuris/](/onuris/).

The docket for this ruling: no false forms on the docket; no contested forms attested; the attestation rests on 4 cited sources — Thinite temple hymns (the Mehyt retrieval), Leiden Return-of-the-Eye cycle (Shu parallel), Abydos and This procession reliefs.
